triage.name: Diarrhea
triage.reason: Extremely common symptom with a structured history, hydration assessment and a wide infectious and non-infectious differential.

demographics: All ages are affected, but incidence is highest in children under 5.
Adults in the US average about one episode of acute diarrhea per year.
Outbreaks occur in daycare centers, long-term care facilities, and after common-source food or water exposures.

risk_factors.text: Ingestion of contaminated food or water
Close contact with a person who has diarrhea
Daycare attendance or exposure to young children
Residence in a long-term care facility or recent hospitalization

social_history: Recent travel to a developing country
Daycare attendance or exposure to young children
Residence in a long-term care facility
Consumption of untreated water or street food
exposures: Recreational water such as pools or lakes

chief_complaints.text: My stools are watery and I can't hold them

hpi.onset: Usually abrupt, beginning within hours after ingestion of the causative agent or medication
hpi.duration: Acute diarrhea typically lasts 1 to 3 days and resolves by 5 to 7 days; symptoms lasting longer than 14 days suggest a persistent or chronic cause
hpi.progression: Starts with loose stools and lower abdominal cramping; stool frequency increases over the first 24 to 48 hours, then decreases. Invasive bacterial or inflammatory causes may progress to fever and bloody stools.
hpi.location: Diffuse or periumbilical; may be lower abdominal
hpi.quality: Watery, loose, or semiformed stools; abdominal discomfort is crampy and intermittent
hpi.severity: Usually mild to moderate; severe dehydration is uncommon in healthy adults
hpi.timing: Intermittent, often worse after meals; nocturnal diarrhea is uncommon and suggests an organic cause

associated_symptoms.text: Urgent need to have a bowel movement

pertinent_negatives: Signs of dehydration such as orthostasis or dry mucous membranes

positives.text: Urgent need to have a bowel movement

argues_against: Severe localized abdominal pain with rebound
Visible blood in stool with high fever
Chronic nocturnal diarrhea with weight loss

atypical.how_it_differs: Infants and young children may present with irritability, decreased wet diapers, and sunken eyes rather than a clear complaint of diarrhea; rotavirus is the most common cause in this group.
missing_classic_features: Clear description of cramping or urgency

atypical.how_it_differs: May have less fever and fewer localizing symptoms, but higher risk of dehydration, medication-induced diarrhea, and Clostridioides difficile infection.
Can have chronic or severe diarrhea from opportunistic infections such as Cryptosporidium or cytomegalovirus; may lack fever despite invasive infection.

general.mild: Well-appearing, alert, normal skin turgor and moist mucous membranes; may be slightly uncomfortable.
general.moderate: Uncomfortable but not toxic; dry mucous membranes, slightly delayed capillary refill, may have mild tachycardia.
general.severe: Ill-appearing, restless or lethargic; markedly dry mucous membranes, sunken eyes, prolonged capillary refill, orthostatic hypotension.
general.critical: Toxic or obtunded; pale, cool extremities, mottled skin, weak peripheral pulses, signs of shock.

findings.finding: Diffuse abdominal tenderness without rebound or guarding

findings.maneuver: Inspect the oral mucosa and tongue
Pinch the skin on the back of the hand or abdomen
Press on the nail bed or fingertips for 5 seconds
Measure blood pressure supine and after standing for 1-2 minutes
findings.finding: Orthostatic hypotension (drop in systolic BP ≥20 mmHg or diastolic ≥10 mmHg)

findings.maneuver: Palpate radial and dorsalis pedis pulses
Ask the patient to cough or gently tap the heel

labs.caveat: Hypokalemia from stool losses; more pronounced with severe watery diarrhea.
Bicarbonate loss in stool can cause a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis.
Elevated from pre-renal azotemia due to volume depletion.
May rise with more severe dehydration; sex-specific normal ranges apply.
Often normal in viral gastroenteritis; elevation suggests invasive bacterial infection.
Elevated in inflammatory diarrhea; helps distinguish invasive from non-invasive causes.
Elevated only with hypoperfusion or sepsis.

imaging.preferred_when: Rarely used; may be considered if bowel obstruction or perforation is suspected.

imaging.study: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Severe abdominal pain, suspected alternative like appendicitis, diverticulitis, or toxic megacolon.

findings.text: Normal or mild diffuse bowel wall thickening
Segmental colonic wall thickening with pericolonic fat stranding
Small bowel inflammation or mesenteric lymphadenopathy

initial.why: Assess electrolytes, bicarbonate, and kidney function; detect hypokalemia, acidosis, and prerenal azotemia
initial.only_if: moderate or severe dehydration, age extremes, or significant underlying illness

initial.why: Leukocytosis with left shift suggests invasive bacterial infection; hemoglobin and hematocrit can reflect hemoconcentration
initial.only_if: bloody stools, high fever, severe abdominal pain, or signs of systemic infection

initial.why: Identifies bacterial pathogens like Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter
initial.only_if: bloody or mucoid stools, fever >101.3°F, severe pain, or outbreak

initial.why: Detects C. difficile toxin; common after antibiotics or hospitalization
initial.only_if: recent antibiotics, hospitalization, chemotherapy, or prior C. difficile
persistent diarrhea >7 days, travel to endemic area, or immunocompromise

confirmatory.test: Multiplex stool pathogen nucleic acid amplification panel
confirmatory.why: Rapidly detects multiple bacterial, viral, and parasitic pathogens
confirmatory.only_if: initial culture negative and pathogen identification needed

supporting.why: Elevated in inflammatory diarrhea; helps distinguish from non-inflammatory
Marker of intestinal inflammation; can guide need for culture

not_indicated.why: Rarely changes management in uncomplicated diarrhea

not_indicated.test: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
not_indicated.why: Not indicated for routine diarrhea; reserve for severe pain or suspected alternative like appendicitis
Not needed unless epigastric pain suggests pancreatitis
Not routinely needed for diarrhea; consider if pregnancy test needed before imaging

decision_points: Assess hydration status and consider oral rehydration before ordering tests in mild diarrhea
Order stool studies only for bloody diarrhea, severe illness, persistent symptoms, or high-risk host
Test for Clostridioides difficile in anyone with recent antibiotics or hospitalization
Consider pregnancy test before imaging in women of childbearing age

differential.name: Clostridioides difficile infection
differential.why_considered: Watery diarrhea after antibiotics or hospitalization, which can look like simple acute diarrhea but can become severe.
differential.trigger: Recent antibiotic use, hospitalization, or chemotherapy with new diarrhea

history: Recent antibiotics, especially clindamycin or fluoroquinolones
Hospitalization or long-term care within the past 3 months
Watery diarrhea, often without gross blood but may be severe
labs: Positive stool C. difficile toxin or PCR
imaging: CT abdomen showing colonic wall thickening and pericolonic stranding
Toxic megacolon (colon diameter >6 cm) in severe cases

differential.name: Ischemic colitis
differential.why_considered: Sudden lower abdominal pain followed by bloody diarrhea in an older adult with vascular risk factors
differential.trigger: Older adult with acute left lower quadrant pain and bloody diarrhea

history: Cardiovascular disease, atrial fibrillation, or peripheral vascular disease
Abrupt crampy pain followed by urge and bloody diarrhea
Prior episodes of abdominal pain after eating
exam: Peritoneal signs only if infarction or perforation
imaging: CT with contrast showing segmental colonic wall thickening, often in splenic flexure or descending colon
Colonoscopy showing cyanotic or ulcerated mucosa, often sparing the rectum

differential.name: Bowel obstruction
differential.why_considered: Abdominal distension, vomiting, and watery stool from overflow around a blockage can be mistaken for infectious diarrhea
differential.trigger: Abdominal distension, vomiting, or prior abdominal surgery with diarrhea

history: Passage of liquid stool around impacted feces
No true increase in stool volume
labs: Elevated lactate if intestinal ischemia develops
imaging: CT or abdominal x-ray showing dilated bowel loops with air-fluid levels
Fecal impaction on rectal exam or imaging

differential.name: Inflammatory bowel disease
differential.why_considered: Recurrent or persistent bloody diarrhea, abdominal pain, and weight loss can be mistaken for acute infectious diarrhea

history: Weeks to months of bloody diarrhea
Family history of inflammatory bowel disease
Extraintestinal symptoms such as joint pain or mouth ulcers
exam: Perianal fissures, fistulas, or skin tags in Crohn disease
labs: Negative stool culture and C. difficile testing
imaging: CT or MR enterography showing bowel wall thickening, skip lesions, or strictures
Colonoscopy with mucosal inflammation, ulcers, and biopsy confirming chronic inflammation

differential.name: Bacterial gastroenteritis
differential.why_considered: Fever, bloody stools, and severe cramping suggest invasive bacterial infection rather than simple viral diarrhea

history: Visible blood or mucus in stool
Undercooked poultry, eggs, unpasteurized dairy, or daycare exposure
labs: Positive stool culture for Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, or Shiga toxin-producing E. coli
Hemolytic anemia and thrombocytopenia can suggest Shiga toxin-producing E. coli
imaging: CT may show nonspecific colonic thickening if obtained for severe pain

differential.name: Celiac disease
differential.why_considered: Chronic watery diarrhea, bloating, and weight loss can be labelled as irritable bowel or recurrent gastroenteritis

history: Chronic diarrhea with pale, bulky, greasy stools
Family or personal history of autoimmune disease
imaging: Small bowel follow-through may show loss of mucosal folds
Duodenal biopsy showing villous atrophy and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes

differential.name: Irritable bowel syndrome
differential.why_considered: Recurrent diarrhea with abdominal pain is a common functional cause

history: Diarrhea alternating with constipation or pain relieved by defecation
Symptoms often worse with stress or certain foods
exam: Normal abdominal exam or mild diffuse tenderness
labs: Normal CBC, CRP, and celiac serologies
imaging: Not indicated unless red flags are present

differential.name: Hyperthyroidism
differential.why_considered: Increased frequency of loose stools with weight loss can be mistaken for chronic diarrhea

labs: Elevated free T4 or free T3
imaging: Thyroid uptake scan only if needed to identify cause

differential.name: Colon cancer
differential.why_considered: Progressive change in bowel habit with blood in stool, anemia, or weight loss in older adults
differential.trigger: Older adult with iron deficiency anemia, positive fecal occult blood, or weight loss and change in stool caliber

exam: Rectal mass on digital rectal exam
labs: Positive fecal immunochemical test or guaiac-based test
imaging: Colonoscopy with mass and biopsy diagnostic
CT abdomen/pelvis may show colonic wall thickening or liver metastases

severity.mild: Acute watery diarrhea, 3-5 bowel movements per day, no or minimal dehydration, normal vital signs, able to maintain oral intake.
severity.moderate: 6-10 stools per day, mild to moderate dehydration (dry mucous membranes, slight tachycardia), some cramping; may need oral rehydration or brief IV fluids.
severity.severe: More than 10 stools per day or dysentery, significant dehydration (orthostasis, oliguria), electrolyte abnormalities, fever, or systemic toxicity; requires IV fluids and possible hospitalization.
severity.critical: Hypovolemic shock, severe metabolic acidosis, altered mental status, toxic megacolon, or sepsis from an invasive pathogen; life-threatening.

red_flags.finding: Visible blood in stool with high fever
red_flags.meaning: Invasive bacterial infection such as Shiga toxin-producing E. coli; avoid antimotility agents and obtain stool culture
Clostridioides difficile infection until proven otherwise

red_flags.finding: Severe abdominal pain, distension, or vomiting
red_flags.meaning: Bowel obstruction, toxic megacolon, or surgical abdomen

red_flags.finding: Orthostatic hypotension, dry mucous membranes, or decreased urine output
red_flags.meaning: Significant volume depletion requiring IV fluids
Higher risk of severe infection, dehydration, and complications

red_flags.finding: Nocturnal diarrhea, unintentional weight loss, or anemia
red_flags.meaning: Chronic organic disease such as inflammatory bowel disease or malignancy
Evaluate for chronic infections, malabsorption, and inflammatory disease

red_flags.finding: Bloody diarrhea with acute left lower quadrant pain in an older adult
Sudden onset severe abdominal pain with shock or acidosis
High fever with bloody diarrhea and decreased urine output in a child
red_flags.meaning: Hemolytic uremic syndrome can follow Shiga toxin-producing E. coli

complications.name: Post-infectious irritable bowel syndrome
clues: Persistent abdominal pain and altered bowel habit after resolution of acute infection

complications.name: Reactive arthritis
clues: Joint pain or swelling 1-4 weeks after bacterial gastroenteritis

special_populations.differences: Dehydration develops more quickly; use oral rehydration solution and monitor wet diapers and tears. Rotavirus is the most common cause in young children.
Higher risk of dehydration, C. difficile, ischemic colitis, and medication-induced diarrhea; may have muted fever and pain.
Dehydration can reduce uterine blood flow and trigger contractions; avoid many antidiarrheals and certain antibiotics; consider listeriosis with fever and diarrhea.
Opportunistic infections such as Cryptosporidium, cytomegalovirus, and C. difficile can cause prolonged or severe diarrhea; lower threshold for stool testing and hospitalization.
Electrolyte and fluid replacement must be adjusted to avoid volume overload and hyperkalemia; acid-base disturbances can worsen rapidly.

key_questions.question: When did the diarrhea start, and how long has it lasted?
key_questions.looking_for: Acute onset with duration <14 days; >4 weeks suggests a chronic cause

key_questions.question: How many loose or watery stools have you had in the last 24 hours?
key_questions.looking_for: At least 3 loose stools per day; high frequency increases dehydration risk

key_questions.question: What does the stool look like—is it watery, greasy, or does it contain blood or mucus?
key_questions.looking_for: Blood or mucus suggests invasive or inflammatory diarrhea; greasy stools suggest malabsorption

key_questions.question: Have you had any abdominal pain? Where is it, and does it improve after a bowel movement?
key_questions.looking_for: Diffuse crampy pain typical of diarrhea; severe localized pain or pain not relieved by stool suggests another cause

key_questions.question: Have you felt nauseated or vomited?
key_questions.looking_for: Vomiting often occurs with viral gastroenteritis; persistent vomiting raises dehydration risk

key_questions.question: Have you had a fever or chills?
key_questions.looking_for: Fever >101.3°F suggests invasive infection; high fever with bloody stool is a red flag

key_questions.question: Have you been able to keep fluids down, and has your urine output decreased?
key_questions.looking_for: Poor oral intake or dark, concentrated, or decreased urine indicates dehydration

key_questions.question: Have you taken any antibiotics in the last 3 months?
key_questions.looking_for: Antibiotic exposure, especially clindamycin or fluoroquinolones, raises risk of Clostridioides difficile

key_questions.question: Have you traveled recently, especially to a developing country?
key_questions.looking_for: Traveler's diarrhea; specific pathogens vary by region and exposure

key_questions.question: Have you eaten any undercooked meat, raw seafood, unpasteurized dairy, or food from a street vendor?
key_questions.looking_for: Foodborne illness; certain foods suggest Salmonella, Campylobacter, or other pathogens

key_questions.question: Has anyone around you had similar symptoms?
key_questions.looking_for: Sick contacts point to viral gastroenteritis or a common-source foodborne outbreak

key_questions.question: Do you have any chronic medical conditions, especially inflammatory bowel disease, celiac disease, diabetes, or an immune problem?
key_questions.looking_for: Comorbidities that increase risk of severe or chronic diarrhea and guide testing

key_questions.question: Are you taking any new medications, including magnesium-containing antacids, metformin, or cancer drugs?
key_questions.looking_for: Medication-induced diarrhea; identifying the culprit may avoid unnecessary testing

key_questions.question: Could you be pregnant?
key_questions.looking_for: Pregnancy affects treatment choices and may require imaging precautions

key_questions.question: Have you noticed any black, tarry stools or blood in the toilet?
key_questions.looking_for: Melena or hematochezia suggests gastrointestinal bleeding or severe infection

key_questions.question: Have you lost weight unintentionally, or do you have diarrhea at night?
key_questions.looking_for: Nocturnal diarrhea or weight loss suggests an organic or malabsorptive disease

reasoning_points: Acute onset of three or more loose or watery stools per day confirms diarrhea.
Duration less than 14 days makes an acute infectious or medication-related cause most likely.
Stool character and the presence of blood or mucus distinguish inflammatory from non-inflammatory diarrhea.
Hydration status is stable: no orthostasis, dry mucous membranes, oliguria, or significant tachycardia.
Recent exposures include sick contacts, travel, undercooked food, or antibiotics, which suggest specific pathogens.
Medication review rules out antibiotics, metformin, magnesium-containing antacids, or other common culprits.
Red flags are absent: severe abdominal pain, high fever, visible blood, persistent vomiting, older age, or immunocompromise.
Key differential includes Clostridioides difficile, bacterial gastroenteritis, inflammatory bowel disease, ischemic colitis, bowel obstruction, hyperthyroidism, and irritable bowel syndrome.
Oral rehydration is appropriate for mild illness; stool studies are reserved for severe, bloody, or persistent diarrhea.

easy: Young healthy adult with abrupt watery diarrhea and vomiting after a viral exposure
No blood, low-grade or no fever, mild diffuse tenderness, no dehydration
Symptoms resolve with oral rehydration within 1-3 days
medium: Traveler with watery diarrhea and mild dehydration requiring oral rehydration and possibly antibiotics
Antibiotic-associated diarrhea with suspected Clostridioides difficile but no severe colitis
Moderate dehydration with orthostasis, hypokalemia, and need for IV fluids
hard: Older adult with sudden left lower quadrant pain and bloody diarrhea, where ischemic colitis must be excluded
Child with bloody diarrhea and decreased urine output, raising concern for hemolytic uremic syndrome
Immunocompromised patient with persistent watery diarrhea from Cryptosporidium or cytomegalovirus
Patient with chronic nocturnal diarrhea, unintentional weight loss, and anemia from inflammatory bowel disease or malignancy
